articles.title: Dogmatic Bayesianism Disorder
articles.content:
Note: This humorously intended sarcastic blog post directly mimics classifications of psychological disorders in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of the American Psychological Association, but Dogmatic Bayesianism is not in the DSM-5 as an actual psychological disorder - for now.

 

Dogmatic Bayesianism Disorder

Diagnostic Criteria                                              F61.1

A. Individuals are convinced that they know what other people want to know.

 

B. Individuals believe that everyone who is not a Bayesian is wrong. They almost continuously try to convince others, and there is often a strong feeling others need to be ‘saved’.

 

C. Strong tendency to ridicule non-Bayesians, including historical figures. Karl Popper (who opposed Bayesianism, as it opens the door to dogmatism in science) is an especially common target.

 

D. A pervasive obsession with Bayesian statistics, and the use of p-values or hypothesis testing by others, at the expense of flexibility, openness, and acknowledging that other coherent statistical approaches exist to deal with uncertainty.

 

E. Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning. The forceful insertion of Bayesian statistics into conversations can drive away conversation partners, to the point where almost all social contact is restricted to other dogmatic Bayesians.

 

F. Individuals believe everyone else will become a Bayesian. Older dogmatic Bayesian often lose bets that everyone will have become a Bayesian by a specific year. If this bet is lost, they continue to claim everyone will become a Bayesian in the future and consider this a rationally updated belief.

 

Specify if:

Persistent: The disorder has been present for more than 12 months.

Specify current severity:

Dogmatic Bayesianism Disorder is specified as severe when an academic exhibits all symptoms of the disorder, at which point individuals are classified as having Bayesian Evangelical Syndrome (BES).

 

Prevalence

Less than 0.01% of the general population is affected, but prevalence is estimated to be at 1% to 2% in statistically inclined academics. Due to diagnostic criterion E prevalence can be up to 80% on certain internet forums. Men are more frequently affected than women, at a ratio estimated at 100:1 or greater.  

Development and course

Development of the condition often starts in the early thirties, but onset can occur at an older age, in which case the symptoms are often much more severe. There is currently no treatment, and dogmatic Bayesianism typically increases with age. In rare cases (less than 1%) spontaneous recovery seems to occur, after which individuals often experience prolonged feelings of shame and embarrassment.

Risk and Prognostic Factors

The disorder is more common in individuals with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

articles.title: On the reliability and reproducibility of qualitative research
articles.content:
With my collaborators, I am increasingly performing qualitative research. I find qualitative research projects a useful way to improve my understanding of behaviors that I want to explore with other methods in the future. For example, some years ago I performed qualitative interviews with researchers who believed their own research had no value whatsoever. Although I did not intend to publish these interviews, they provided important insights for other projects that I am engaged in now. I was involved in qualitative research on the assessment process of interdisciplinary research (Schölvinck et al., 2024), and we performed interviews to understand how researchers interpret a questionnaire we were developing that measures personal values in science (Kis et al., 2025). Together with Anna van ‘Veer I supervised Julia Weschenfelder who interviewed scientists on what they believed the value of their research was, and I have hired Julia as a PhD as part of a large project on the meaningful interpretation of effect sizes. She is planning interviews with researchers about what determined the maximum sample size they are willing to collect (if you want to be interviewed about this, reach out!). With Sajedeh Rasti, who is completing her PhD in my lab, we have spent the last 2 years interviewing people who played important roles in the creation of large-scale coordinated research projects in science.

As a supervisor, I am always very actively involved in research projects, and I joined as many of the (extremely interesting) interviews Sajedeh performed, and I listened to the audio recordings of all interviews that Julia performed to give my interpretation of what the scientists discussed when interviewed. Yet it never occurred to me to independently perform the thematic analysis for these interviews, and compare the themes we derived. I became aware of this peculiarity after reading a great qualitative paper analyzing open questions in a study on questionable research practices (Makel et al., 2025). In this paper, two teams independently analyze themes in the same set of open questions. They largely find the same themes, and conclude: “our two independent analysis teams reported themes that were generally similar or overlapping, suggesting a robustness of the findings. We believe this suggests that independent qualitative analyst teams with similar positionality can use unique analytic paths and reach largely similar destinations. This contributes to the ongoing conversation within the qualitative research community about whether reproducibility and replicability are relevant or possible in qualitative research”.


Sometimes you read a paper that makes perfect sense – of course two independent teams should reach the same conclusions when they qualitatively analyze the same data – and yet, it was not part of your workflow. This is especially peculiar, because we use this exact workflow when we code other data sources. For example, Sajedeh Rasti will soon share a preprint on papers written by large teams of scientists. In this paper, we classify these papers into different categories, depending on the interdependencies that require coordination (e.g., epistemic, logistical, financial, etc., see Rasti et al., 2025). Sajedeh and I double-coded papers, and we discussed our levels of agreement. This is the normal thing to do. It is strange that I never considered the same approach when the data comes from interviews.

 

Research on inter-rater reliability of thematic coding

I looked into the literature to search for papers similar to Makel et al., 2025, where the same qualitative data is analyzed by multiple coders to examine how reproducible the themes are that are identified in the data. There are many more papers than the few I will list here, and someone should write a paper summarizing this literature. But this is a Sunday morning blog post, and not a systematic review, so I will just present some papers that I found interesting.

Armstrong and colleagues had six researchers independently analyze the same single focus‑group transcript, and found “close agreement on the basic themes,” but substantial divergence in how those themes were interpreted and organized, with each analyst having “‘packaged’ the themes differently.” (Armstrong et al., 1997). The authors in this paper then go on and say these differences demonstrate the inherent subjectivity in qualitative research. But this is not the message I take away from this paper at all. All coders of any type of data will differ slightly in the details they highlight. What matters most in this project is not how in verbal summaries of the themes, researchers highlight different details – that is to be expected, but also largely irrelevant – but that there is such clear agreement on the themes identified. If I read the examples in the paper, the differences are mainly in detail, where some summarize the themes at a higher level, and others on a more detailed level. Those who summarize the themes at a detailed level will of course pick out specific details others did not mention – but this can easily be improved upon by instructing coders better about the level of detail at which results should be provided, and how details should be chosen in verbal summaries.

Campbell and colleagues (2013) provide a great example of the work needed to reach high inter-rater reliability. They say that “Reliability is just as important for qualitative research as it is for quantitative research” and argue that replicability problems stem less from disagreement over themes per se than from “the unitization problem—that is, identifying appropriate blocks of text for a particular code or codes,” which can “wreak havoc when researchers try to establish intercoder reliability for in-depth semistructured interviews.” Using their own empirical coding exercise, they show that even with a detailed codebook, intercoder reliability remained modest (“54 percent reliability on average”), reflecting the interpretive complexity of semistructured interviews where “more than one theme and therefore more than one code may be applicable at once.” However, when disagreements were resolved through discussion, intercoder agreement rose dramatically to 96%, and 91% of initial disagreements were resolved. In my view, qualitative research is nothing special in this respect, as it is often difficult to achieve high inter-rater reliability in any coding project. For example, we have the same difficulty in reaching agreement when we code what the main hypothesis in a scientific paper is in metascientific research projects (Mesquida et al., 2025).

The importance and challenges of clear coding instructions related to text-segmentation is also discussed in a classic paper on the reliability qualitative research (MacQueen et al., 1998). Based on extensive experience with qualitative research at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, MacQueen and colleagues offer useful suggestions on creating a codebook that will lead to high reliability. Through an iterative process in which multiple coders independently code the same text, compare results, and revise definitions, they show how disagreement over themes is an indication of ambiguous codes – and not an inherent limitation of qualitative research. Reproducibility can be achieved by repeatedly checking whether coders can “apply the codes in a consistent manner” and refining the codebook until agreement is acceptable. The authors argue that we should not expect that coders will naturally “see” the same themes, but that they can code the same themes reliably if researchers use a disciplined, transparent, and collective codebook development process that supports reproducible qualitative analysis without denying its interpretive character.

A realist ontology in qualitative research

The idea of reliability, or reproducibility (the two concepts become intertwined in a lovely way in qualitative research, as the coder is the measurement device, so to say) in qualitative research emerges most naturally from a scientific realist perspective on knowledge generation. There are qualitative researchers who adopt philosophical perspectives that attempt to argue reliability and reproducibility are not relevant for qualitative research. I have engaged with these ideas a lot over the years, and find them unconvincing. Seale and Silverman (1997) push back strongly against the idea that reliability would not apply in qualitative research, and write “We believe that such a position can amount to methodological anarchy and resist this on 2 grounds. First, it simply makes no sense to argue that all knowledge and feelings are of equal weight and value. Even in everyday life, we readily sort fact from fancy. Why, therefore, should science be any different? Second, methodological anarchy offers a clearly negative message to the audiences of qualitative health research, suggesting that its proponents have given up claims to validity.”

I am personally more sympathetic to the view expressed by Popay and colleagues (1998): “On one side, there are those who argue that there is nothing unique about qualitative research and that traditional definitions of reliability, validity, objectivity, and generalizability apply across both qualitative and quantitative approaches. On the other side, there are those postmodernists who contend that there can be no criteria for judging qualitative research outcomes (Fuchs, 1993). In this radical relativist position, all criteria are doubtful and none can be privileged. However, both of these positions are unsatisfactory. The second is nihilistic and precludes any distinction based on systematic or other criteria. If the first is adopted, then, at best, qualitative research will always be seen as inferior to quantitative research. At worst, there is a danger that poor-quality qualitative research, which meets criteria inappropriate for the assessment of such evidence, will be privileged.” There are unique aspects of reliability in qualitative research, but qualitative research will not be taken seriously by the majority of scientists if researchers do not engage with reliability at all.

O’Conner and Joffe provide a useful guide on how to achieve inter-coder reliability in qualitative research in psychology, based on their own extensive experience (O’Connor & Joffe, 2020). They argue that “ICR helps qualitative research achieve this communicative function by showing the basic analytic structure has meaning that extends beyond an individual researcher. The logic is that if separate individuals converge on the same interpretation of the data, it implies “that the patterns in the latent content must be fairly robust and that if the readers themselves were to code the same content, they too would make the same judgments” (Potter & Levine-Donnerstein, 1999, p. 266).” They highlight how there are both external incentives to care about reliability (as it can function as a signal of quality) but also has direct benefits for the researchers performing the qualitative research.

If you feel similarly, and want to educate your students about qualitative methods where reliability and reproducibility are important, there is a nice paper that can be used to introduce your students to realist ontologies in qualitative research by Lourie and McPhail (2024). They note how the methodology literature in qualitative research often engages with interpretivist-constructivist approaches. Among my own collaborators, this perspective is not seen as appealing, and we prefer to build our qualitative research from a realist ontology. In this philosophy, inter-rater reliability, and reproducibility, are important aspects in knowledge generation (Seale, 1999). A good textbook on applied thematic analysis from this perspective is Applied Thematic Analysis (Guest et al., 2012).

I am very grateful to Makel and colleagues for making me realize I had overlooked the importance of independent coding of themes in qualitative research, and establish inter-rater reliability or reproducibility in qualitative research.

 

Personal take-home messages

After reflecting on this topic, there are some points that I am taking away from the work on reliability or reproducibility of thematic coding.

First, independent thematic analysis, and comparing how we code qualitative data, should be a standard practice in the qualitative studies in my lab. The suggestions by MacQueen and colleagues provide useful guidance that we should follow. There is nothing special about qualitative data sources in this respect.

Second, we already ask all participants if we can share full transcripts, and many agree. In our case, as we primarily interview scientists, so we are in the lucky position that they value transparency and data sharing, and that the content of our interviews is not particularly sensitive. Data sharing is of course not always possible. For example, in my interviews on why researchers felt their own research lacked any value whatsoever, many did continue to receive funding for this research, and they would not want their actual thoughts about their research to become public. But where possible, we should share transcripts for independent re-analysis and re-use.

Third, we should use the same techniques to increase the reliability of our claims in qualitative research, as we do in quantitative research. I recently have been annoyed by some extremely biased qualitative studies in metascience, where the researchers who performed the research clearly wanted their work to lead to a very specific outcome. It is easy to tell the story you want in qualitative research, if you reject the idea of reliability. But in my lab, we use methods that prevent us from allowing us to say what we want to be true, if we are wrong. In my current research project, I reserved 8000 euro out of the 1.5 million euro budget to hire ‘red teams’ (Lakens, 2020) to criticize the studies before we perform them. However, I had planned to only use red teams for large quantitative studies. I now think that I should also use the red teams for the qualitative studies I planned in the proposal, to make sure the coding of themes is reliable.

 

References

Campbell, J. L., Quincy, C., Osserman, J., & Pedersen, O. K. (2013). Coding In-depth Semistructured Interviews: Problems of Unitization and Intercoder Reliability and Agreement. Sociological Methods & Research, 42(3), 294–320. https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124113500475

articles.title: New Papers: Optimal Filter Settings for ERP Research
articles.content:
Zhang, G., Garrett, D. R., & Luck, S. J. (in press). Optimal filters for ERP research I: A general approach for selecting filter settings. Psychophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14531 [preprint]

Zhang, G., Garrett, D. R., & Luck, S. J. (in press). Optimal filters for ERP research II: Recommended settings for seven common ERP components. Psychophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14530 [preprint]

What filter settings should you apply to your ERP data? If your filters are too weak to attenuate the noise in your data, your effects may not be statistically significant. If your filters are too strong, they may create artifactual peaks that lead you to draw bogus conclusions.

For years, I have been recommending a bandpass of 0.1–30 Hz for most cognitive and affective research in neurotypical young adults. In this kind of research, I have found that filtering from 0.1–30 Hz usually does a good job of minimizing noise while creating minimal waveform distortion.

However, this recommendation was based on a combination of informal observations from many experimental paradigms and a careful examination of a couple paradigms, so it was a bit hand-wavy. In addition, the optimal filter settings will depend on the waveshape of the ERP effects and the nature of the noise in a given study, so I couldn’t make any specific recommendations about other experimental paradigms and participant populations. Moreover, different filter settings may be optimal for different scoring methods (e.g., mean amplitude vs. peak amplitude vs. peak latency).

Guanghui Zhang, David Garrett, and I spent the last year focusing on this issue. First we developed a general method that can be used to determine the optimal filter settings for a given dataset and scoring method (see this paper). Then we applied this method to the ERP CORE data to determine the optimal filter settings for the N170, MMN, P3b, N400, N2pc, LRP, and ERN components in neurotypical young adults (see this paper and the table above).

If you are doing research with these components (or similar components) in neurotypical young adults, you can simply use the filter settings that we identified. If you are using a very different paradigm or testing a very different subject population, you can apply our method to your own data to find the optimal settings. We added some new tools to ERPLAB Toolbox to make this easier.

One thing that we discovered was that our old recommendation of 0.1–30 Hz does a good job of avoiding filter artifacts but is overly conservative for some components. For example, we can raise the low end to 0.5 Hz when measuring N2pc and MMN amplitudes, which gets rid of more noise without producing problematic waveform distortions. And we can go all the way up to 0.9 Hz for the N170 component. However, later/slower components like P3b and N400 require lower cutoffs (no higher than 0.2 Hz).

You might be wondering how we defined the “optimal” filter settings. At one level, the answer is simple: The optimal filter is the one that maximizes the signal-to-noise ratio without producing too much waveform distortion. The complexities arise in quantifying the signal-to-noise ratio, quantifying the waveform distortion, and deciding how much waveform distortion is “too much”. We believe we have found reasonably straightforward and practical solutions to these problems, which you can read about in the published papers.

articles.title: Seeing Without Seeing: A Methodological Review of Visual Mental Imagery Reconstruction from Brain Activity
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.13691v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstructing visual mental imagery from brain activity differs from reconstructing perceived images. Imagery is generated top-down, its signal is weak, and the imagined content is never observed, so decoders are trained and scored against a proxy such as a cue or a seen exemplar. This criterion-guided methodological review of mainly non-invasive studies (fMRI, EEG, MEG) is narrative rather than systematic. We organise the field into a two-stage pipeline, two design axes and four method families, and formalise target-free evaluation, in which the proxy gap is a systematic bias rather than noise. A two-dimensional admissibility criterion crosses trial-level separability from working-memory maintenance with the memory source of the imagined content. Among the studies reviewed, every image-scored reconstruction concerns a recalled exemplar, none builds a scorable target for concept-generated content, and all come from fMRI, consistent with missing image-level targets in electrophysiological data. Published values for five decoders, compared under a common human forced-choice framing, show seen-to-imagined drops of 5.9 to 26.1 percentage points and a change in method ordering. We treat this as a diagnostic signal, not a controlled benchmark result, and specify a within-subject test for an altered neural code. Beyond this synthesis, we make two proposals. First, because frozen generative priors can produce photorealistic images weakly tied to neural signals, we combine existing null-signal controls into a normalised neural dependence with a within-category null, an unvalidated diagnostic quantity. Second, we propose a candidate ten-item reporting checklist with illustrative pass criteria. In an exploratory application to ten studies, none reports all items in a fully checkable form; this describes reporting practice, not study quality.
articles.author: Shiyi Zhang, Dong Liang, Yihang Zhou

articles.title: How Well Do Benchmarks Evaluate LLMs' Use for Personal Health Informatics?
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.13652v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmarking is a valuable technique for advancing the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), including in personal health informatics. There are growing efforts on benchmark creation for personal health data activities. However, it is unclear whether and how well these efforts align with needs and considerations of personal health informatics process. Addressing this need, we first analyzed 53,587 tasks across eight benchmarks related to personal health informatics and characterized the space of benchmark design. We then contrasted our observations of design choices with personal informatics theories and empirical knowledge. We find significant mismatches between existing benchmark design and domain guidelines and understanding. This lack of alignment limits the utility of the evidence current benchmarks offer about LLM capabilities. We use domain knowledge to highlight capabilities benchmarks should include and discuss opportunities our work enables for taking a human-centered and domain-driven approach to benchmark design.
articles.author: Fatemeh Mirhosseini, Yasaman S. Sefidgar

articles.title: EyeQ: Exploring Corneal Reflection for Mobile Context Sensing
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.13640v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: What if a single face-facing camera could sense your surroundings---through your eyes? We introduce EyeQ, which explores corneal reflection as a modality for context-aware mobile interaction. Traditional vision-based context sensing relies on world-facing cameras that demand explicit aiming or dual-camera setups; EyeQ instead shows that an off-the-shelf VLM can read scene context from corneal reflections captured with a smartphone camera. To recover usable detail from mobile corneal crops, EyeQ pairs on-device iris-guided capture with server-side AI enhancement, then leverages VLMs to extract scene types, names, and objects from warped, unfamiliar eye-image sequences. In an N=10 study, we characterize how capture conditions shape reflection fidelity, evaluate what VLMs detect, misclassify, and hallucinate, and demonstrate interaction opportunities, including detecting a steering wheel to distinguish drivers from passengers. This work reframes the eye in HCI---from a target for gaze estimation to a passive mirror of one's surroundings---and examines the privacy tensions it raises.
articles.author: Jaewook Lee, Judith Amores, Donghoon Shin, Bo-Eun Choi, Jason Kim, Davin Win Kyi, Seok-Young Kim, Jon E. Froehlich, Andrew D Wilson

articles.title: EJAI: Judgment-Preserving Civic AI for Data Center Environmental Justice
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.13525v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Communities in the United States and around the world are contesting data centers, the physical infrastructure of AI. These disputes pose environmental justice issues: residents must weigh unevenly distributed burdens using evidence scattered across metrics, corporate claims, policy documents, and public testimony. A formative study with 10 users showed that dashboards and single-agent AI can settle questions before people examine that evidence. Here we present EJAI, a source-grounded system that links an interactive map, retrieved evidence, missing-data statements, and two stakeholder personas that allow people to inspect evidence and form their own policy recommendations. In a small functional benchmark of 21 queries, retrieved evidence supported 98.4% of factual claims and the system acknowledged missing evidence in 32 of 33 cases. Persona alignment carried a grounding cost: the Corporate Executive omitted some evidence that conflicted with its assigned priorities. In a within-subjects study, 15 participants acting as residents prepared for a simulated town hall. Some checked cited AI claims while treating map metrics as official, some made conditional recommendations with safeguards such as water-use disclosure, and some found the personas simplified or biased. Our results suggest that civic AI can support preparation for public reasoning when it makes evidence, gaps, and disagreement open to inspection, and that corpus imbalance and two-sided personas remain open justice concerns.
articles.author: Evan Pa\v{c}es-Wiles, Bryen Alvarez, Sara Gulabani, Akshara Kolipaka, Snehalkumar 'Neil' S. Gaikwad

articles.title: Towards Accessible, Autonomous Photosynthesis Monitoring on Living Leaves
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.13387v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Photosynthesis is a direct biomarker of plant health and functioning. However, measuring net photosynthesis on individual leaves requires expensive (USD 42,000 - USD 89,000) instruments and manual effort. This limits access to photosynthesis sensing and makes long-term monitoring across multiple leaves difficult. We present a 1000x low-cost, autonomous sensing system that enables longitudinal monitoring of photosynthesis on living leaves over multiple days. Guided by a formative user study with 13 plant biology researchers, the system integrates an automated, leaf-attached chamber with a low-cost CO2 sensor. Built using a 3D-printed clamp and thermoformed dome, the chamber periodically closes to measure CO2 drawdown and reopens to refresh the air. Each chamber costs about USD 62 and operates independently, allowing multiple leaves to be monitored simultaneously without pumps or gas tubing. We characterize each chamber and validate its measurements against a research-grade gas exchange instrument (CIRAS-4) across 29 sessions (R^2 = 0.90). We also demonstrate monitoring of C3 and CAM photosynthesis plants, adaptability to different leaf geometries, and a light-response experiment. In a nine-day deployment, six chambers captured simultaneous CO2 exchange from individual leaves of the same plant during drought and rewatering. Each leaf showed different patterns of nighttime CO2 uptake and recovery, which a whole-plant CO2 measurement instrument would obscure. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of such leaf-level photosynthesis dynamics using independent, low-cost autonomous chambers. Our work opens new opportunities for plant science, education, and data-driven agriculture.
articles.author: Qitong Li, Xiaoyu Zheng, Xuanang Chen, Julia Wang, Raj Nileshbhai Dave, Dayanara Chavez, Nirvik Prakash Iyer, Nivedita Arora

articles.title: Designing Accessible and Rigorous ML Experiments: No-Code Visual Workflows and Structured Guidance for Beginners
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.13386v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Designing machine learning (ML) experiments requires beginners to plan a methodologically sound workflow and implement it in a concrete environment. We evaluated two forms of support in two within-participant studies with 18 predominantly technically trained participants: mlguide, which provides structured, evidence- backed guidance for workflow design, and AI Sandbox, a visual no-code environment for workflow implementation. After using mlguide, participants produced better high-level workflow designs, but their scores on a quiz about specific methodological choices did not improve significantly. Compared with Google Colab, AI Sandbox received higher hedonic user experience ratings, while perceived workload and acceptance did not differ significantly. These findings suggest that different forms of interactive support help with differ- ent aspects of beginner ML experimentation. The paper contributes a reusable evaluation task with instructions, a modified dataset, and a quiz, as well as empirical evidence on structured guidance for workflow design and on the experience of implementing workflows in visual and notebook-based environments.
articles.author: Henrik H. J. Detjen, David Pfrang, Max Westphal, Melissa Finster, D\"orte Corr, Markus Wenzel

articles.title: Ender: Visual Scaffolding for Geometric Proof Comprehension
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.13368v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Geometric proof is a foundational but notoriously difficult topic in secondary mathematics, primarily due to the high cognitive load required to integrate visual diagrams with logical text. As proofs evolve, tracking the initial givens and an expanding set of derived truths can easily overwhelm working memory. While established scaffolding techniques are often visual and diagram-based, current digital learning environments mostly rely on static, text-heavy interfaces that force students to manage these complex mental models on their own. This paper introduces Ender, an interactive rendering system designed to visualize the logical status of two-column proofs. Ender's design is grounded in four literature-derived requirements: (1) diagram annotation, (2) structural tracing, (3) support for partial or incorrect work, and (4) synchronization between the diagram and text. To evaluate the system, we conducted a between-subjects, think-aloud experiment with 12 secondary school students in the United States, comparing Ender against a traditional digital proof interface. Our results indicate that students using Ender performed significantly better on proof comprehension tasks--specifically in identifying and correcting logical errors. These findings suggest that dynamic visual scaffolding may ease the working memory burden of digital interfaces, offering a promising building block for future AI-based proof tutoring systems.
articles.author: Hwei-Shin Harriman, Yuchen Jin, Dominik Moritz, Joshua Sunshine

articles.title: Project Progress Desk: Know Where All Your Claude Code and Codex Projects Stand at a Glance
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.13287v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Codex and Claude Code let developers work on many projects in parallel, but keeping track of them still means switching between chats, terminal sessions and providers. We present Project Progress Desk, a local desktop interface that brings overall progress, blockers and pending decisions into one view. Users can see which projects need attention, inspect what remains, and compare earlier approaches before choosing how to continue. Agent receipts link reported outcomes to each project's weighted acceptance checklist; the overview distinguishes receipt-supported progress from dated estimates. We describe daily use across 36 projects, including a choice between two implementations based on their recorded outcomes. At the demo, attendees will explore 30 simulated projects, trace completed work to overall progress, and watch a coding agent's new result update the overview.
articles.author: Wanghao Ye, Yiting Wang, Shwai He, Guoheng Sun, Ziyao Wang, Yexiao He, Zheyu Shen, Zhaoyi Liu, Bowei Tian, Daeun Jung, Aditya Sarkar, Parastoo Pilevar, Xiaochuan Gong, Yancheng Zhu, Yingying Fan, Qiong Wang, Yuning Zhang, Meng Feng, Siyuan Peng, Zhenle Duan, Sihan Chen, Ziyi Wang, Yifei Dong, Yilong Dai, Ang Li

articles.title: Designing UIs with GenAI: Understanding the Use, Benefits, and Limitations of Prompt-to-Design Generators
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.13211v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The integration of generative AI (GenAI) into user interface (UI) design has led to prompt-to-design generators (P2dGens), tools that enable designers to create UI prototypes from textual prompts efficiently. Despite their growing adoption, little is known about how designers use these tools in everyday practice, their benefits, and limitations. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 17 UI designers to investigate P2dGens use, focusing on workflow integration, attitudes toward generator-assisted design, and the organizational climate. Findings show that designers primarily use P2dGens as ideation accelerators rather than end-to-end solutions, and they adopt a variety of individual and collaborative prompting strategies. Designers expressed complex attitudes, noting gains in efficiency and inspiration while also highlighting concerns about loss of personal creativity and design quality. We also observed emerging governance practices and varying attitudes within organizations toward P2dGens. These insights illuminate how P2dGens reshape UI design workflows and contribute to understanding human-AI collaboration in UI design.
articles.author: Jingzhou Ye, Yao Li, Xueqiang Wang

articles.title: TypedInk: Knowing When Not To Draw
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.13027v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can a scientific figure generator know when it does not have enough evidence to draw? Complete-source illustrators map a finished methodology section to a schematic, or a table to plotting code, and are never asked this question because their input is assumed complete. The research record is rarely that complete: an outline, a draft paragraph, a table, or a one-sentence intent, in any combination, and painting measured numbers with an image model when the table is missing is a hallucinated result. TypedInk infers a figure type from {diagram, plot, plate} from a possibly incomplete source and dispatches to the renderer that can honor that type's evidence contract, refusing dispatch when the contract cannot be met. On the six gold plots in TypedFigBench (5 views, n=30), TypedInk's code path inks every gold table token when a table is observed (12/12), refuses the 12 hidden-table views instead of inventing numbers, and marks 6 intent-only views illustrative, with no execution failures. An always-draw coder with no such gate inks 30/30 charts, including all 18 with no table, and recovers zero gold numbers on any of them; two vision-language raters (not humans; human replication is future work) still judge those always-draw charts submittable 17/36 times, against TypedInk's refusal 0/36 times. A diagnostic field ablation of the type router (16 illustrations, 5 views each, n=80) locates where this failure would originate if unchecked: an outline alone yields type accuracy 0.31 and sends every gold plot into an integrity violation, and a chat-model planner narrows but does not close the gap (overall accuracy 0.85, still integrity-failing on 25% of outlines). Diagram-label recall is 0.47 on the full record and 0.19 on an outline. Gold plates are typed at dispatch (oracle integrity-fail 0.00) and rendered as stills.
articles.author: Weiwei Yang

articles.title: Orthographic depth at two scales, with English also matched for lexicon size
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.13400v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: A reader can struggle to read in only one of their languages, and one proposed reason is how predictably spelling maps to sound. We measure that predictability as conditional entropy, the pronunciation uncertainty left once the spelling is seen, at two grain sizes (unit sizes): the alignment unit, an aligned spelling-sound chunk, and the syllable, bounded in the pronunciation. We analyse word lists in twelve alphabetic orthographies and report five in full, with English pronunciations from a dictionary and the rest from the synthesizer eSpeak-ng, length marks removed. Among the five, English has the most uncertainty and Finnish the least at both grains. Across all twelve, Portuguese and Danish exceed English per alignment unit, and German and Italian order differently by grain and transcription. These orders hold when English is transcribed by eSpeak-ng with u allowed to spell /j/ plus a vowel. Uncertainty per unit has no shared direction as units grow: it falls in Spanish and, less securely, German, is level in Finnish, depends on transcription in Italian and on the word list in English, and rises in Norwegian and Swedish. Summed uncertainty per word falls in all twelve, but that score is handed the pronunciation's boundaries and mixes context with in-sample memorisation, so it is no evidence of what a reader computes. An exact identity states when discarded spelling boundaries could reverse that fall. A uniform 20,000-word English sample holds 35% of the dictionary's syllable spellings and has syllable entropy 0.098 bits lower, so lexicons must be matched in size. In an exploratory check over eleven languages, syllable-scale entropy tracked first-year reading accuracy (rho = -0.74, falling to -0.25 if English is given the lowest entropy instead), without separating the syllable scale from the alignment unit. These estimates describe sampled writing systems, not readers.
articles.author: Adam Y. Shavit

articles.title: IC-GNN: Modeling Individualized Brain Community Organization for Disease Prediction
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.13070v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Brain networks exhibit modular organization, where community structures vary substantially across individuals and diseases. Understanding these individual differences is crucial for advancing both basic neuroscience research and precision medicine. However, widely used predefined group-level brain atlases often overlook this heterogeneity. While individualized functional parcellations capture subject-specific variability in community boundaries, they often require lengthy scan times to achieve fine-grained resolution and complicate cross-subject comparisons. To address this trade-off and investigate how individualized community organization captures disease-associated changes across individuals, we propose IC-GNN, an atlas-anchored model that forms distinct, individualized functional communities directly over atlas-defined brain regions. IC-GNN derives discrete, individualized multiscale communities from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, refines community-guided connections, and adapts shared regional weights to each subject's community context to enable both individualized modeling and group-level comparisons. Across more than 30,000 participants from ABIDE (autism spectrum disorder), ADNI (Alzheimer's disease), and the UK Biobank (depression), IC-GNN achieves the highest performance compared with 15 baseline methods. We further demonstrate that these individualized communities are reproducible within scans and across sessions, and carry predictive power on their own. Furthermore, IC-GNN identifies disease-related shifts in community organization that align with established literature, highlighting a promising approach for modeling individualized community structure for disease prediction and biomarker discovery.
articles.author: Yang Zhang, Xiao Zhou, Jonathan Warrell, Avram Holmes, Xuan Zhang, Mark Gerstein, for the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative

articles.title: Predicting Time-to-conversion for Dementia of Alzheimer's Type using Multi-modal Deep Survival Analysis
articles.content:
arXiv:2205.01188v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Dementia of Alzheimer's Type (DAT) is a complex disorder influenced by numerous factors, but it is unclear how each factor contributes to disease progression. An in-depth examination of these factors may yield an accurate estimate of time-to-conversion to DAT for patients at various disease stages. We used 401 subjects with 63 features from MRI, genetic, and CDC (Cognitive tests, Demographic, and CSF) data modalities in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database. We used a deep learning-based survival analysis model that extends the classic Cox regression model to predict time-to-conversion to DAT. Our findings showed that genetic features contributed the least to survival analysis, while CDC features contributed the most. Combining MRI and genetic features improved survival prediction over using either modality alone, but adding CDC to any combination of features only worked as well as using only CDC features. Consequently, our study demonstrated that using the current clinical procedure, which includes gathering cognitive test results, can outperform survival analysis results produced using costly genetic or CSF data.
articles.author: Ghazal Mirabnahrazam, Da Ma, C\'edric Beaulac, Sieun Lee, Karteek Popuri, Hyunwoo Lee, Jiguo Cao, James E Galvin, Lei Wang, Mirza Faisal Beg, the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative

articles.title: Differential Diagnosis of Frontotemporal Dementia and Alzheimer's Disease using Generative Adversarial Network
articles.content:
arXiv:2109.05627v2 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease are two common forms of dementia and are easily misdiagnosed as each other due to their similar pattern of clinical symptoms. Differentiating between the two dementia types is crucial for determining disease-specific intervention and treatment. Recent development of Deep-learning-based approaches in the field of medical image computing are delivering some of the best performance for many binary classification tasks, although its application in differential diagnosis, such as neuroimage-based differentiation for multiple types of dementia, has not been explored. In this study, a novel framework was proposed by using the Generative Adversarial Network technique to distinguish FTD, AD and normal control subjects, using volumetric features extracted at coarse-to-fine structural scales from Magnetic Resonance Imaging scans. Experiments of 10-folds cross-validation on 1,954 images achieved high accuracy. With the proposed framework, we have demonstrated that the combination of multi-scale structural features and synthetic data augmentation based on generative adversarial network can improve the performance of challenging tasks such as differentiating Dementia sub-types.
articles.author: Da Ma, Donghuan Lu, Karteek Popuri, Mirza Faisal Beg

articles.title: Grey matter sublayer thickness estimation in themouse cerebellum
articles.content:
arXiv:1901.02499v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The cerebellar grey matter morphology is an important feature to study neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease or Down's syndrome. Its volume or thickness is commonly used as a surrogate imaging biomarker for such diseases. Most studies about grey matter thickness estimation focused on the cortex, and little attention has been drawn on the morphology of the cerebellum. Using ex vivo high-resolution MRI, it is now possible to visualise the different cell layers in the mouse cerebellum. In this work, we introduce a framework to extract the Purkinje layer within the grey matter, enabling the estimation of the thickness of the cerebellar grey matter, the granular layer and molecular layer from gadolinium-enhanced ex vivo mouse brain MRI. Application to mouse model of Down's syndrome found reduced cortical and layer thicknesses in the transchromosomic group.
articles.author: Da Ma, Manuel J. Cardoso, Maria A. Zuluaga, Marc Modat, Nick. Powell, Frances Wiseman, Victor Tybulewicz, Elizabeth Fisher, Mark. F. Lythgoe, Sebastien Ourselin

articles.title: Optimization principles, revisited
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.14381v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The brain solves a wide range of problems, and some of these solutions are very good indeed. It is an old idea that, in some cases, these solutions may be as good as possible given the relevant constraints. If this is true we can promote this notion of optimization to a principle from which aspects of function and mechanism can be derived, ideally with no free parameters. Optimization principles are powerful and have had many successes, but they remain controversial. We start with a reminder of a classic example---diffraction limited optics in insect eyes---and then a summary of why you should worry about optimization as a more general principle. Next we turn to recent progress on the theory of optimal motion estimation in fly vision, and finally summarize recent results on the landscape for optimization, arguing that (contrary to widely held intuitions) optimal performance need not require the underlying mechanisms to have finely tuned parameters. I hope to convince you that this is a moment to take optimization seriously as the basis for theories of neural coding and computation. This is based on a rather informal lecture at the summer school LASCON X in Sao Paulo, and I have tried to preserve that tone here; pointers are given to more detailed and technical discussions.
articles.author: William Bialek
